content_summary.text: In 2024 property taxes were 'an average of 28.4 percent of local funding nationally'; more than half of local revenue in NH, CT, NJ and ME, under 15 percent in AR, AL and NV.

Fall 2026 ballot initiatives 'from Florida to Wyoming' would cut local revenue; major reforms already passed since 2023 in 'more than a dozen states, including Georgia, Texas, Wyoming, and Iowa' (those four are NOT named as Nov 2026 measures).
Earlier 1970s-80s revolt included 'California's Proposition 13 and Massachusetts' Proposition 2 1/2'; the article gives no 1978 date or other years.

Home prices 'have skyrocketed more than 50 percent since January 2020'; 'property taxes nationwide have increased only slightly more than overall inflation since 2020'; homeowners 'often think they do' rise with values.
If a locality leaves its rate unchanged as values rise 'the result is a silent tax increase'.

Florida Amendment 3: non-school homestead exemption to $250,000 by 2028; assessment cap on non-homestead from 10 to 5 percent; restricts spending of property-tax revenue; tasks legislature with raising exemption to full assessed value.
Tax Foundation's Jared Walczak: replacing 'more than $42 billion' (full Florida elimination) would require average state-local sales tax from 7.02 to 15.34 percent.

content_summary.grep: fell short of making the ballot
content_summary.text: Ohio abolition amendment 'fell short of making the ballot this November'; Walczak working paper: sales tax 5.75 to 13.36 percent or income tax 2.75 to 8.24 percent to replace $21 billion.

content_summary.grep: limiting the amount by which the levy
content_summary.text: North Carolina amendment requires legislature to 'enact general laws limiting the amount by which the levy of taxes on property may increase'; article notes it 'includes no specifics'.
Wyoming Initiative 1 would exempt half of a homestead's assessed value statewide; outgoing Republican governor warned of an 'immediate and devastating effect'.

Assessment limits are 'one of the most problematic' tools; LA example: $5,212 vs $11,172 on two $947,000 homes; Prop 13 cap 'lesser of 2 percent or the rate of inflation'; Florida homestead cap lesser of 3 percent or inflation since 1995.

Adam Langley (Lincoln Institute): absent state funding, statewide homestead exemptions of '$20,000 to $40,000' are about right; Florida's is unique in mandating a high exemption with no state reimbursement.
Recommended alternatives: circuit breakers (more than a dozen states), deferrals, homestead exemptions (30+ states), truth-in-taxation laws (20 states).

content_summary.grep: supply of land can’t be increased
content_summary.text: On land: 'the supply of land can't be increased or reduced in response to a tax'; the property tax 'at least the part levied on unimproved land, doesn't distort behavior'; a combined land-and-buildings tax is still more efficient than sales or income tax. This is the article's ONLY land-tax content: it never uses 'land value tax' or 'split-rate' (grep returns zero).

existing_wiki_coverage: Searched digest.md and repo. events/proposition-13.md covers 1978 Prop 13 mechanics, lock-in, Prop 2 1/2 in one sentence (Legacy and Spread) and ends with a See Also line pointing to places/wyoming; it has no section on the 2026 wave. places/wyoming.md already carries the Wyoming Initiative 1 details (50% exemption, SoS fiscal note $92.6m FY2028) and cites Ballotpedia for 13 measures in 7 states (FL, GA, LA, NC, OK, TN, WY). research/lincoln-ohio-property-tax-alternatives.md already carries Walczak's Ohio replacement-rate figures (8.24% income, 13.36% sales). research/cabral-hoxby-hated-property-tax.md covers salience. events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md mentions the Ohio abolition measure only via Blessing's SJR 7 quote. No page covers Florida Amendment 3 or the NC levy-limit amendment. Zero hits for 'Gorey', 'Land Lines revolt', 'Amendment 3' outside places/wyoming. Not already in the wiki: Florida Amendment 3 provisions, NC amendment, the LA/Miami assessment-limit disparity illustrations, the national 28.4% local-reliance figure.
uncertainties: The assignment text suggested the article names Michigan, North Dakota, Texas and Georgia ballot measures: it does not. Georgia, Texas, Wyoming and Iowa appear only as states that already enacted reforms since 2023; Michigan and North Dakota do not appear at all. The three live measures it names are Florida Amendment 3, a North Carolina levy-limit amendment and Wyoming Initiative 1; Ohio's failed to qualify.

The article does not date Prop 13 (1978) or Prop 2 1/2 (1980) and does not discuss 'assessment lag' or 'rate-vs-levy confusion' by name; salience is implicit ('highly visible') and the rate-vs-levy point appears as the 'silent tax increase' passage. Grep 'land value' and 'split' return zero hits: nothing on LVT or split-rate as a response, only the efficiency remark on unimproved land.
Byline mismatch: the page shows 'By Jon Gorey' but the Yoast JSON-LD metadata lists author 'Katharine Wroth' (grep 'Katharine Wroth' in gorey.html). Cite the visible byline plus institution.

The '$42 billion' figure is attributed to Walczak/Tax Foundation but is not in the linked Tax Foundation pages that were saved; T1 should hedge or omit the figure. The 7.02 to 15.34 percent figure is in the saved Tax Foundation text (grep '15.34').

Florida facts beyond the article (EDR scores ~ $12 billion recurring local revenue loss; court-ordered ballot-language rewrite) come from Florida Policy Institute (advocacy/think-tank, Tier 2) in the saved voter guide; use only as origin, not as support.
Chart data and the Case-Shiller/FRED series behind the 50-percent figure were not independently retrieved.

content_summary.text: LIMS history: Introduced by Councilmember Nadeau 14 Jul 2026; Notice of Intent to Act published 24 Jul; Notice of Public Hearing filed 1 Sep; 'Referred to Committee of the Whole' 22 Sep; 'Public Hearing on B26-0777' 16 Oct 2026. Committee of the Whole referral only; no committee report listed.
Referral to Committee of the Whole dated 22 Sep 2026 on LIMS (the Secretary's memo is dated 16 Jul: grep 'July 16, 2026' in dc-lims-b26-0777-memorandum.txt).
Hearing: 10:00 a.m., Friday 16 Oct 2026, Room 412 (Track B), John A. Wilson Building; 'Revenue Proposals for the Fiscal Year 2028 Budget'.

content_summary.grep: Transitioning to a land value tax (Bill 26-777)
content_summary.text: The seven proposals include 'Transitioning to a land value tax (Bill 26-777)', a new business activity tax, a wealth proceeds tax (Bill 26-749), pied-a-terre, sales, real property and income tax proposals.
'This hearing is limited to invited witnesses and agency representatives; however, anyone may submit written testimony.' Record closes 5:00 p.m. Friday 30 Oct 2026 (grep 'October 30, 2026').

content_summary.grep: not intended to be a referendum
content_summary.text: 'This hearing is not intended to be a referendum to gauge popular support.'

Bill text: for tax year beginning July 1, 2028, land component 'shall reflect the estimated market value of the land as if vacant and available for its highest and best use'; quarterly installments from same year (grep 'quarterly in four equal installments'); ratio studies to include 'a separate land value component'; effective after 30-day congressional review.

Nadeau's Statement of Introduction: changes would 'improve the long-term fiscal health of the District without changing rates or increasing taxes'; cites 1997, 2014 and 2024 Tax Revision Commissions (grep 'This aligns with proceedings') and Maryland and Virginia having authorized local LVT.

content_summary.grep: respectfully oppose the land value assessment provisions
content_summary.text: Litkenhous: 'I respectfully oppose the land value assessment provisions of Bill 26-777 and any transition to a citywide land value tax or split-rate property tax.' Recommends striking the provisions, considering quarterly billing separately, improving Class 3/4 tools, and requiring a parcel-level study.

Zoning: DC Policy Center 2019 'found that only about 36 percent of nearly 118,000 examined tax lots potentially had room for growth under existing zoning'; '71 percent of the District's more than 93,000 single-family lots faced a high zoning barrier'. Testimony adds 'Those figures are generous'.
'Where development cannot proceed, the tax is not an incentive. It is a penalty for owning land in Washington.' (line-wrapped in the PDF text: grep 'is not an incentive')

Valuation: OTR uses the income approach for most income-producing property, a methodology that 'does not naturally separate the contribution of land from the contribution of improvements'; too few clean vacant-land comparables.
content_summary.locator: 'Valuation Concerns' (spans pp3-4; grep 'for most income-producing property' for the line before)

content_summary.grep: returned to a single-rate system in 2001
content_summary.text: Pittsburgh 'returned to a single-rate system in 2001 ... after a countywide reassessment sharply increased land values and triggered public opposition' (cites Lincoln Institute PDF).
Triple-net leases pass property tax to tenants; a highest-and-best-use land assessment 'can tax the unrealized redevelopment potential' beneath small businesses.

'September 2026 estimate from the Office of the Chief Financial Officer ... total real property tax liability is down about 5 percent', driven by declining commercial/office values (source not independently fetched).
Existing tools: Class 3 vacant and Class 4 blighted rates, 'recently refined ... through D.C. Law 26-41 with a newly graduated tax rate schedule' (not independently checked).

content_summary.grep: only about 36 percent potentially could have room for growth
content_summary.text: DC Policy Center 2019 primary: 'Of the nearly 118,000 tax lots for which we could make a determination, only about 36 percent potentially could have room for growth under current zoning laws'; nearly 60 percent of ~7,600 commercial buildings and about 60 percent of 16,376 multifamily buildings potentially have room; 93,835 single-family lots, 71 percent high barrier.

DC Policy Center's own 2019 conclusion: 'Still, a land value tax could be a worthwhile reform' (introduction) -- the testimony cites the 36 percent figure but not this conclusion or the ~60 percent commercial/multifamily room figures.

Sayin (DC Policy Center) testimony: of 4,110 lots of 25,000 sq ft or more, 315 privately owned, vacant and potentially buildable; 'Only 22 of them sold in the last two years'; OTR values about 21,100 properties on income.

Sayin: taxing land more heavily 'has intellectual merit' but she is 'not convinced that the District can produce land assessments reliable enough to administer a fair tax system, especially for income-producing properties'; recommends narrowing to low-density residential areas and excluding income-producing commercial and multifamily property.

content_summary.grep: failure of the assessment system, not of the idea
content_summary.text: Sayin on Pittsburgh: it 'used a split-rate tax for nearly 90 years before abandoning it in 2001 ... That was a failure of the assessment system, not of the idea.' 12 active split-rate jurisdictions, mostly small Pennsylvania cities.

content_summary.grep: The law already requires separate land and building values
content_summary.text: Sayin: 'The law already requires separate land and building values' (D.C. Code section 47-821), but OTR has focused on the total value -- a qualification to the wiki page's framing of what the bill adds.

ArentFox Schiff (secondary): supporters GGWash and 'several academic experts' citing Detroit; skeptics 'the CFO, a real estate appraiser, and the National Taxpayers Union Foundation'; CFO said LVT 'would require an entirely new assessment methodology' (grep 'entirely new assessment methodology'). Not found in the CFO's written testimony.
Hearing featured CFO testimony 'and more than 20 invite-only public witnesses'; shortfall roughly $700 million; Mendelson said the proposals are for the FY2028 budget.

uncertainties: Official hearing record (witness list, transcript/video, other testimony PDFs, any committee report or fiscal impact statement) could not be reached; the hearing section can state the notice and bill facts firsthand but witness lists rest on secondary coverage (ArentFox, Washington DC Magazine Substack, 7News, Nadeau press release). Cavalry's characterisation of the DC Policy Center is selective: it uses the 36 percent all-lots figure, which is dominated by 93,835 single-family lots, but the same DCPC piece reports roughly 60 percent of commercial and multifamily buildings potentially having room and concludes an LVT 'could be a worthwhile reform' while 'will do little to increase the housing supply' where supply is short. 'Those figures are generous' is the testifier's own judgment. T1 should state the DCPC figures from DCPC, not from the testimony.

The CFO's remark that a land value tax would need a new OTR assessment methodology is reported only by ArentFox Schiff; the CFO's written testimony does not contain it (likely oral Q&A). Attribute to the law firm's summary or omit.
Cavalry's claims 'OCFO September 2026 estimate: liability down about 5 percent' and 'D.C. Law 26-41' graduated vacant-property schedule were not verified against primaries.

Cavalry earns fees from property tax assessment appeals (testimony states ~two decades representing taxpayers in appeals): a conflict of interest that is stated in the testimony itself; the wiki should describe the firm as a commercial real-estate tax advisory firm, not as neutral experts.

LIMS 'Referred to Committee of the Whole' 22 Sep vs Secretary's memo 16 Jul (to the Chairman referring to COW): the exact referral date on the wiki page should follow LIMS and say 'introduced 14 July; referred (per LIMS 22 September)' or avoid the issue.
Cavalry's Sept post says it 'posted arguments against ... back in September'; the Cavalry post date listed on the page is 19 Oct 2026, the hearing 16 Oct.
